fatal_errors: The alloy is incorrectly assumed to be single-phase and homogeneous; the target material was an as-cast, solidification-segregated two-BCC-phase alloy with W-Ta-rich dendrites and Zr-Ti-rich interdendritic regions.
The proposed 800–1000 °C tensile/creep regime does not reconstruct the reported room-temperature compression, room-temperature-to-500 °C indentation, and room-temperature scratch tests.

Lattice distortion is asserted as the cause of enhanced ductility and toughness, although the target work associated it primarily with strengthening and did not experimentally isolate it as the cause of plasticity or crack resistance.
The cited evidence does not establish fracture-toughness enhancement or the proposed mechanism at 800–1000 °C.
explanation: The response addresses the correct broad comparison and predicts greater plastic strain and toughness than commercial tungsten, so it is relevant and scientifically conceivable. However, it substantially departs from the target material state, test methods, and temperature range. It omits the two-phase dendritic segregation that is central to the actual alloy and substitutes a hypothetical homogeneous, grain-size-matched material. Its mechanism also conflates strengthening by lattice distortion with the origins of damage tolerance; the target interpretation instead invoked Ti, V, and Zr effects, localized plasticity, grain-boundary cohesion, and impeded crack propagation, while acknowledging that these causes were not directly isolated. The proposed experiment has some discriminating value, but comparing compositionally different materials cannot by itself isolate lattice distortion, and dislocation density or activation volume is not a unique signature of that mechanism. E3 supports dislocation-mediated indentation creep only over approximately 298–573 K, while E1 and E2 provide broad application context rather than direct support for the claimed toughness mechanism.
